answer.label: Not Mark Twain — a 20th-century proverb he never wrote
answer.authorDates: Popularized 20th c. · wrongly pinned on Mark Twain (1835–1910)
answer.sourceLine: There is no substantive evidence Mark Twain ever wrote or said this. Per Quote Investigator ↗, the “rhymes” formulation emerged decades after his 1910 death and was first credited to Twain only in 1970. The earliest strong match is psychoanalyst Theodor Reik in 1965 (“history … merely rhymes”); no precise author is confirmed. Twain did write a thematically related aphorism in his 1873 novel The Gilded Age, but it used kaleidoscope imagery, not the rhyming metaphor.

source.excerpt: History never repeats itself, but the Kaleidoscopic combinations of the pictured present often seem to be constructed out of the broken fragments of antique legends.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive evidence Twain made the “rhymes” remark, which appears only after his 1910 death.
The earliest strong match is Theodor Reik’s 1965 essay “The Unreachables”: “It has been said that history repeats itself. This is perhaps not quite correct; it merely rhymes,” per QI ↗.
Twain was first credited in 1970 by Canadian artist John Robert Colombo, who told QI he had seen the saying as anonymous “proverbial lore” in the 1960s, per QI ↗.
Twain’s genuine related line appears in The Gilded Age (1873) ↗ and uses kaleidoscope imagery, not rhyme.
source.excerptNote: Twain’s actual 1873 aphorism from The Gilded Age — related in spirit but worded quite differently from the compact “rhymes” proverb later attached to his name.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is a 20th-century proverb with no confirmed author or first-publication source, so no copyright status can be asserted. Twain’s genuinely authored 1873 line in The Gilded Age is public domain, but that is a different sentence; the 1965 Reik formulation, if treated as the origin, would be in copyright.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: About Mark Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain — pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens — was the American author of The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, celebrated for his sharp, aphoristic wit. That reputation makes him a magnet for feel-good sayings he never wrote. He did coin a genuine cousin of this line in The Gilded Age (1873), but not the “rhymes” version now stamped with his name.

misattribution.heading: How Twain got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most confidently mis-cited lines. The wording is genuinely clever, so it drifted onto Twain — but the paper trail runs the other way.

items.why: Twain died in 1910; the earliest known appearance of a matching sentence is Theodor Reik’s in 1965, and no source in Twain’s writings contains it, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Canadian artist Colombo printed the saying under Twain’s name in Neo Poems (1970); asked in 2011, he said he’d met it as anonymous “proverbial lore” in the 1960s and never had a real source, per QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Twain’s real contribution is the different, kaleidoscope-imagery line in The Gilded Age (1873) ↗; the compact “history rhymes” proverb has no confirmed author.

context.heading: Why the line sticks
lead: The aphorism endures because it captures a real idea — that historical events echo without exactly recurring — in a single memorable image. That very quotability is what let it float free of any author and settle on the most quotable name available.

Twain is the default magnet for orphaned wit, and because he really did write a near-neighbor sentence about history not repeating, the mistaken credit feels plausible enough that few readers check it.
context.pull: A near-miss line by Twain, plus his reputation for wit, made a proverb no one can source look like vintage Twain.
